context: Ad-Dukhan is Makkan and short, and it addresses people who had heard the message and treated it as entertainment. It opens on the night the Qur'an came down and closes by telling the Prophet ﷺ to watch, since they are watching too. Between those points it sets one warning beside another with almost no connective argument.

Its central image, a smoke covering the people, was read two ways by the earliest authorities and still is. Ibn Mas'ud held that it had already come, in the famine that struck Quraysh so hard that a hungry man looking up saw something like smoke between himself and the sky, and his explanation is recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari. Others read it as a sign still ahead, and a report in Sahih Muslim lists a smoke among the signs preceding the Hour. The matter is disputed, and the surah does not settle it.
name_story: Named from verse 10, where the sky is told to bring a visible smoke that covers the people. The word occurs once and the surah is named for it, which is a fair guide to how the surah operates: one image, held long enough that what follows it becomes the real subject. Under the smoke people say plainly that they believe, and the answer given is that a clear messenger had already reached them.

movements.h: The night the Book came down
movements.note: An oath by the clear Book, then the statement that it was sent down on a blessed night in which every wise matter is made distinct. The passage grounds the revelation in mercy from a Lord who gives life and takes it.

movements.h: Smoke, and a promise made under it
movements.note: The deniers are left in their amusement and told to watch for a sky bearing visible smoke. They will ask for the torment to be lifted and will declare themselves believers. The lifting is described as brief, and a greater seizure is named after it.

movements.h: Pharaoh, and a sea left as it was
movements.note: Musa asks that the servants of Allah be handed over, then is told to travel by night and to leave the sea as it was, because the army behind him is to be drowned. What that court left behind of gardens, springs, crops and pleasant places is inventoried, and the surah says heaven and earth did not weep for them.

Quraysh demand their ancestors be produced as proof of resurrection. They are asked whether they are better than the people of Tubba', a title borne by kings in Yemen, and told that the heavens and the earth were not created in play.
Zaqqum is described as the food of the sinful, boiling in bellies like scalding water. The man being dragged is addressed with the very titles of honour he once claimed for himself.

movements.h: A secure place, and one death only
movements.note: Those who feared Allah are placed in gardens and springs, in fine silk, tasting no death beyond the first. The surah ends by saying the Qur'an has been made easy on the Prophet's ﷺ tongue, and telling him to watch.

themes.d: The plea under the smoke is a complete profession of belief, and it is refused, because a clear messenger had already come and been dismissed. This surah measures belief by when it arrives, not by how it is worded.

Revelation descends on a night in which every wise matter is made distinct. Most commentators identify it as the Night of Decree in Ramadan, in line with the statement elsewhere that the Qur'an was sent down in Ramadan; a minority among the early authorities placed it in mid-Sha'ban, and the majority did not accept that.
Verse 29 is among the coldest lines in the Qur'an. A regime holding gardens, springs and noble estates is removed, and the only comment offered is that the sky and the earth did not weep for them.

The demand to watch a resurrection happen now is met with the purpose of creation instead of a demonstration. If the heavens and earth were not made as amusement, a day of settled accounts is not an extra claim but the thing that makes the rest hold together.

heart: Ad-Dukhan can be recited in a single sitting, and its pace is what a reader notices first. It moves without transition from a night of decree to a smoke, from a drowning to a tree, from the tree to silk and springs. Nothing is developed or explained. Taking it slowly leaves each image standing on its own, which is how it was built.

Most readers stop at the plea made under the smoke, because it is the prayer anyone would make and it comes too late to count. Reciting that verse with attention raises a plain question about the timing of one's own return, and the surah does not soften it. What it does instead is end on the far side, in a place of safety where the only death ever tasted is the one already behind.

passages.why: The descent of the Qur'an is placed on a blessed night in which every wise matter is separated out. Read with the statement that the Qur'an was sent down in Ramadan, this is the ground of what is sought in the last ten nights.
The words of people asking for the torment to be lifted and promising belief. Worth pausing on because the wording of the plea is faultless and it changes nothing.
Heaven and earth did not weep for them. One sentence measures what a power that ruled a whole country was actually worth.
The reply to a demand for resurrection on request. Creation was not play, and this is one of the most compact statements of that argument anywhere in the Qur'an.

connections.why: Al-Qadr names the night that Ad-Dukhan describes and adds what descends on it. Commentators read each in the light of the other, and neither is complete alone.
Ash-Shu'ara gives the exchange between Musa and Pharaoh at length. Ad-Dukhan compresses it to a dozen verses and keeps the ending, so reading them in sequence shows what the compression is for.

virtue.text: No authentic report establishes a specific merit for reciting Ad-Dukhan. A report does circulate about reciting it on the night before Friday, with forgiveness promised or angels seeking forgiveness for the reciter; it is found in Jami' at-Tirmidhi, who called it gharib himself, and later hadith critics graded it weak. It is not relied on here. The authentic material touching this surah concerns what the smoke refers to, which is a question of meaning and not a reward for recitation.
virtue.src: no authentic prophetic virtue report; the Friday-night report in Jami' at-Tirmidhi is graded weak
